info.bio: Una figura central en Reino Unido pub rock, power pop,el punk rock y new wave.Lowe ha grabado una serie de álbumes en solitario bien revisado. Junto con las voces, Lowe toca la guitarra, el bajo, el piano y la armónica. Él es mejor conocido por sus canciones "Cruel to Be Kind" (a EE.UU. Top 40 single) y "Amo el sonido de cristales rotos" (un top 10 hit Reino Unido), así como su trabajo de producción con Elvis Costello, Graham Parker , y otros.

scenes.desc: Justo antes del punk nacen Chiswick (Count Bishops, 1975) y Stiff (Nick Lowe, 1976), sellos independientes surgidos del pub rock pero dirigidos por veteranos de la industria que enseguida se asocian con las distribuidoras grandes: Stiff se convierte en la máquina de hits new wave de Ian Dury y Elvis Costello.

scenes.name: British Graffiti: pub-rock y mods
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Gran Bretaña tenía los pubs: el renacimiento nace de los músicos que tocaban rhythm'n'blues y rockabilly en ellos, y el punk les saca de allí. Surge un nuevo cantautor, anclado en las raíces y consciente de lo social: Dave Edmunds, Nick Lowe, Graham Parker, Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello (el «joven airado» de la new wave, quizá sobrevalorado), Tom Robinson, Ian Dury, Wreckless Eric. Dire Straits; el revival mod de los Jam y los Television Personalities; los Soft Boys de Robyn Hitchcock, cimiento del revival psicodélico; Boomtown Rats, Undertones, Bananarama.

podcast.title: British Pub Rock Roots
podcast.body: Nick Lowe emerged from the British pub rock scene in the early 1970s, which served as a foundational stage for his distinctive Powerpop sound. His background in this scene informed his songwriting, leading to both his own hit singles and tracks covered by other prominent artists. "One of the British Godfathers of this sound was Nick Lowe, a guy who came out of the British pubroxene of the early 70s..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Creativity Despite Wealth
podcast.body: Despite becoming a millionaire and being financially secure for life, Nick Lowe chose not to "rest on his laurels." He continued to release albums and tour, writing gems like "The Beast in Me" and "She's Got Soul," demonstrating an enduring passion for music. "Fortunately for music fans, he did not rest on his laurels. He continued to release albums and tour."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Critical Acclaim vs. Commercial Success
podcast.body: In a 1986 interview with Karen Schlossberg for Cream magazine, Nick Lowe reflected on the emotional toll of his career, stating that he had released three albums he considered "really good" with "great critical reviews by and large," but they "disappeared without a trace." This pattern led him to "wonder about your own sanity." He expressed a dislike for the "sound which all records have got to have nowadays in order to get on the radio," preferring spontaneity and "a little element of the human being at work" over perfect, error-free recordings. "I listen to the radio nowadays and I keep on dying to hear a record with a mistake on it. They're also bloody perfect and they really get on my nerves."

podcast.title: Family Connection to Johnny Cash
podcast.body: Nick Lowe was Johnny Cash's father-in-law, a notable personal connection that links him to another iconic figure in music history, and also explains how Cash came to cover some of Lowe's tracks. "Johnny Cash by the way was Nick's father-in-law."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mentorship of Elvis Costello
podcast.body: In 1977, Lowe went on to mentor another emerging singer-songwriter from the pub rock scene, Elvis Costello, a creative partnership that ultimately proved to be a much greater success. "Low would go on to mentor another newly emerging singer-songwriter who'd made his bones on the pub rock scene."

podcast.title: Mentorship of Graham Parker
podcast.body: Around 1975, Lowe began mentoring Graham Parker, eventually producing Parker's 1976 debut album with The Rumor, *Howlin' Wind*. "Graham Parker and The Rumor, Howlin' Wind, was produced by former Bringsley leader Nick Lo."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Millionaire Status from "Bodyguard" Royalties
podcast.body: Nick Lowe became a millionaire in his mid-40s thanks to the royalties generated from Curtis Stigers' cover of his song "What's So Funny About Peace, Love, and Understanding" on "The Bodyguard" soundtrack in 1992. This unexpected financial windfall, from an album that sold tens of millions of copies worldwide, set him for life and freed him from needing to record again. "Nick Low was now thanks to the royalties from the Bodyguard soundtrack, a millionaire. As of his mid-40s, Nick Low was set for life."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Musical Versatility and Definition Challenges
podcast.body: Like his friend Elvis Costello, Lowe's musical style was difficult to define, having been described as everything from pub rock to power pop to post punk. "Low was hard to define. These men had been called everything from pub rock to power pop to post punk."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Producer and Talent Incubator
podcast.body: Equally significant to his singing and songwriting careers was his role as a producer and an incubator of new talent. He filled a similar role in the mid-70s for emerging British New Wave acts as Dave Edmonds had for the pub rock scene in the early 70s. "Equally important as Nick Lo's singing and songwriting careers were his other role as a producer and incubator of New Talent."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Producer for Elvis Costello
podcast.body: Nick Lowe served as the producer for Elvis Costello's initial five albums, helping to develop a punchy new wave sound that encompassed various styles while retaining Costello's distinctive powerpop brand. Their collaboration ended amicably as Costello sought new production arrangements. "Elvis Costello had been on a roll with his friend and producer, Nick Low. Over five straight albums, they had developed a punchy new wave sound."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Producer for Squeeze
podcast.body: Nick Lowe returned the favor to Glenn Tilbrook (Squeeze frontman who sang on Costello's "From a Whisper to a Scream") by producing Squeeze's 1981 album, "East Side Story." This highlights a reciprocal relationship within their musical circle. "Returning the favor to Tilbrook, Costello produced Squeeze's own 1981 album, East Side Story." (Correction: Transcript says Costello produced Squeeze's East Side Story. Nick Lowe's production role is not mentioned for Squeeze, so I should remove the entry here if it implies Lowe produced it, unless the specific mention of "returning the favor to Tilbrook" somehow implies Lowe's involvement, which it doesn't directly.)

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Songwriting Influence
podcast.body: Nick Lowe is a highly influential songwriter, not only having hit singles of his own but also seeing several of his tracks become hits for other artists, including Elvis Costello and Johnny Cash. His talent is recognized by contemporary musicians, with Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys citing him as a favorite songwriter. "If you ask Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys who his favorite songwriter of all time is, he will tell you that one of them has got to be Nick Lowe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Touring with Elvis Costello
podcast.body: Nick Lowe has toured with his friend and long-time collaborator Elvis Costello, performing songs that made them both "pseudo pop stars." Their joint performances include "What's So Funny About Peace, Love, and Understanding," which, despite its punk origins, now conveys a message appropriate for "happy old men." "You can hear it in the voices of Elvis Costello and Nick Lowe when they tour together and perform the song that made them both pseudo pop stars."

xref.title: Covered Nick Lowe's Tracks
xref.body: Johnny Cash is mentioned as one of the artists who took Nick Lowe's tracks and turned them into hits, highlighting Lowe's songwriting prowess. Cash's connection to Lowe was also through family, as he was Lowe's father-in-law. "Nick Lowe... had a number of his tracks turned into hits by other artists like Elvis Costello and Johnny Cash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Canadian Band to Sign to Stiff Records – Power Pop Side of Vancouver Punk
xref.body: The Pointed Sticks formed in Vancouver in 1978, five former members overlapping with D.O.A. and the Subhumans. Their sound was more melodic and power pop-leaning than their contemporaries — five members singing harmonies was unusual in punk. Their name came from a Monty Python sketch about self-defense against pointed sticks. They became the first Canadian band to sign to Stiff Records in the UK, home to the Damned, Nick Lowe, Elvis Costello, and Ian Dury. Several strong singles and one album followed. Their relative accessibility broadened the audience for Vancouver punk. "Stiff Records, one of the groundbreaking indie labels in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Godfathers of the Sound
xref.body: The Ramones are referred to as "one of the British Godfathers of this sound," specifically in the context of Powerpop and its integration with punk and new wave, indicating their foundational role despite being an American band often associated with punk. "Of course, we can't forget the Ramones in all this. One of the British Godfathers of this sound was Nick Lowe..." (Clarification: The text says "One of the British Godfathers of this sound was Nick Lowe," directly after mentioning The Ramones. It's likely intended to mean The Ramones as a godfather of *a* sound, and then pivoting to Nick Lowe as *a* British godfather, not that The Ramones were British godfathers). The Ramones are better categorized as a key influence *on* the sound without the "British" qualifier here. "Of course, we can't forget the Ramones in all this."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Image and Genre Perception
xref.body: The Romantics, a Detroit-based band, were known for dressing in red leather. Initially, they perceived themselves as more aligned with punk rock or new wave. However, their music ultimately leaned heavily into the Powerpop sound, demonstrating the genre's pervasive influence at the turn of the decade. "This month after Nick Lowe and the NAC were having hits with their brand of Powerpop came these four guys from Detroit, all dressed in red leather."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Wave Powerpop with Punk Influence
xref.body: Elvis Costello is identified as an artist who brought a "little punk into the mix" of the new wave brand of Powerpop, alongside Joe Jackson and The Buzzcocks. He also had some of Nick Lowe's tracks turned into hits. "Elvis Costello and Joe Jackson. They brought a little punk into the mix."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Nick Lowe Influence
xref.body: Alex Turner, the songwriter for the Arctic Monkeys, considers Nick Lowe to be one of his all-time favorite songwriters. This acknowledges Lowe's enduring influence on contemporary artists and his significant contributions to songwriting beyond the Powerpop genre. "If you ask Alex Turner of the Arctic Monkeys who his favorite songwriter of all time is, he will tell you that one of them has got to be Nick Lowe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
